participantInstructions: You will have 30 minutes to read the 21st Century Skills, the Performance Indicators, and the Case Study Situation for this event. You will then have up to 15 minutes to present your recommendation to the judge; no additional time is allotted for judge questions, which the judge may ask within the presentation itself. Both members of your participant team must take part in the presentation and in answering the judge's questions. You will be evaluated on how well your presentation and your answers meet the performance indicators listed below. Turn in all of your notes and materials to the judge when you have finished.
situation:
You and your partner serve as the director of technical programs and the compliance and purchasing coordinator at KEELSON TRADE COOPERATIVE, a for-profit vocational school owned outright by the instructors and staff who work there. The board chair (judge) has called a meeting ahead of the next membership vote and has asked your team to bring a recommendation on a decision that has already split opinion among the co-op's worker-owners.

KEELSON trains welders, electricians, and HVAC technicians across three campuses and answers to the state's technical-school licensing board for its safety record. For eleven years the cooperative has bought welding helmets, gloves, and respirators only from COASTAL SAFETY SUPPLY, a five-person family shop that built its business around Keelson's account. The purchase contract gives Keelson the right to audit Coastal's safety certifications and sourcing records at any time, a right no purchasing coordinator has ever exercised.

Six students in the spring welding cohort reported that a new batch of auto-darkening lenses fogged and failed mid-arc, and two suffered minor flash burns before the helmets were pulled from the shop floor. Two of the injured students have been hesitant to describe what happened, worried it will affect their standing in the program, and drawing out a full account has taken patience and encouragement. The compliance coordinator suspects Coastal switched to a cheaper lens subcontractor after losing another client, and that an audit would expose the solvent-disposal records for the coating process, regulated as hazardous waste.

Coastal's owner mentioned, off the record, that losing Keelson's account, sixty percent of its revenue, would force layoffs among its four other employees. Keelson's own bylaws direct worker-owners to put student safety first, but several members who trained alongside Coastal's founder argue a private warning and a real chance to fix the defect is the fairer opening move toward a partner never before questioned. Waiting risks another injury before the fall cohort starts, while auditing immediately risks ending a decade of loyalty and triggers a report to the licensing board either way.

The board chair (judge) wants the team to recommend whether to invoke the audit clause immediately or give Coastal a defined window to correct the lens defect before deciding further, and to explain, since the compliance coordinator would sign as the cooperative's authorized agent either way, how that decision should be delivered to Coastal's owner and to the students who were hurt.

The board chair (judge) will open the meeting by greeting the participant team and asking to hear its recommendation and the reasoning behind it. The team should be ready to describe how it weighed the co-op's obligation to its students against its obligation to a partner that has served it well for over a decade. The board chair (judge) will thank the team once the presentation and any questions are finished.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the board chair (judge) of KEELSON TRADE COOPERATIVE, elected by the membership to oversee governance between annual meetings. Business background is the same as the situation above. You have asked the director of technical programs and the compliance and purchasing coordinator to recommend whether the cooperative should invoke its long-unused audit clause against COASTAL SAFETY SUPPLY now or give the vendor a defined window to correct the welding-helmet defect first, and how that decision should be communicated to Coastal's owner and to the students who were hurt.

During the presentation, ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: What would you say to Coastal's owner if the audit ends up forcing the co-op to end an eleven-year contract?
What would you say to the students who were burned if the co-op decides to give Coastal more time before acting?
